sections.heading: What is Bit Manipulation?
sections.content: Bit manipulation works directly on the binary representation of numbers using bitwise operators (AND, OR, XOR, NOT and shifts). Because these operations run in a single CPU instruction, they let you solve some problems in O(1) time and O(1) space that would otherwise need loops, extra arrays or hash sets. Bits are also a compact way to represent a set of up to about 20 to 30 items as a single integer (a bitmask), which makes subset enumeration and bitmask DP possible.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Find the element that appears an odd number of times, or the missing or duplicate number, with O(1) extra space
Check, set, clear or toggle a particular bit; count set bits; test for a power of two
Represent a small set (up to about 20 to 30 elements) as an integer bitmask
Enumerate all subsets or submasks of a set
Bitmask DP: states described by which items are already used (traveling salesman, assignment)
Binary tries and maximum XOR problems
Arithmetic without operators, fast multiply or divide by powers of two
Keywords: single number, XOR, power of two, number of 1 bits, bitmask, subset, binary representation, without using + or -

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Think of an integer as a row of light switches. Each switch is a bit that is either 1 (on) or 0 (off). AND keeps a switch on only if it is on in both rows, OR turns a switch on if it is on in either row, and XOR turns a switch on only when the two rows differ. Shifts slide the whole row left or right, which doubles or halves the number. A handful of tiny tricks built from these moves, such as n and (n - 1), cover most interview problems.

sections.heading: Basic Operations in Code
sections.code:
val a = 0b1011                     // 11
val b = 0b0110                     // 6

println(a and b)                   // 2   (0b0010)
println(a or b)                    // 15  (0b1111)
println(a xor b)                   // 13  (0b1101)
println(a.inv())                   // -12 (flips all 32 bits)
println(a shl 2)                   // 44
println(a shr 1)                   // 5
println((-8) shr 1)                // -4  (sign is kept)
println((-8) ushr 28)              // 15  (zeros are shifted in)

// Binary strings and parsing
println(Integer.toBinaryString(11))        // 1011
println(Integer.parseInt("1011", 2))       // 11

// Represent a set of elements 0..n-1 as one Int (or Long for up to 63 elements)
var set = 0
set = set or (1 shl 3)                         // add element 3
set = set or (1 shl 5)                         // add element 5
val has5 = (set and (1 shl 5)) != 0            // membership test
set = set and (1 shl 3).inv()                  // remove element 3
val size = set.countOneBits()                  // number of elements
val union = set or 0b1010
val intersection = set and 0b1010
val difference = set and 0b1010.inv()
val isSubset = (set and 0b1010) == set         // is 'set' contained in the other mask?

sections.code:
fun isPowerOfTwo(n: Int): Boolean = n > 0 && (n and (n - 1)) == 0

fun isPowerOfFour(n: Int): Boolean =
    n > 0 &&
    (n and (n - 1)) == 0 &&                    // exactly one set bit
    (n and 0x55555555) != 0                    // and that bit is at an even position (0, 2, 4, ...)
// Time: O(1)   Space: O(1)

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting parentheses: Kotlin infix functions such as and, or, shl all share one precedence level and are evaluated left to right
Using shr instead of ushr when you want zeros shifted in for negative numbers
Using 1 shl i with i >= 31 on an Int (it overflows to a negative number); use 1L shl i with a Long
Shift counts are taken modulo 32 for Int (and 64 for Long), so x shl 32 equals x
Using && or || on integers; the bitwise operators are and, or, xor
Calling x and -x on Int.MIN_VALUE and expecting a positive result
Using bitmasks for more than about 20 to 25 items (the 2^n states become too large)
Forgetting that XOR tricks need the 'everything else appears an even or fixed number of times' guarantee
Dividing negative numbers with shr and expecting rounding toward zero (shr rounds toward negative infinity)

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Bitwise operators work on the binary form of numbers in O(1) time
XOR cancels equal pairs, which solves 'find the odd one out' problems with O(1) space
x and (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, and x and -x isolates it
A bitmask is a compact set: bit i means item i is in the set, enabling subset enumeration and bitmask DP
Always parenthesize bit expressions in Kotlin, and use ushr for zero-fill shifts
Use Long (1L shl i) when you need more than 31 bits, and avoid bitmasks beyond about 20 to 25 items
